originalTitle: Ukraine’s dismissed defence minister calls for wartime presidential election
summary: Mykhailo Fedorov’s appeal is most direct challenge to Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russian invasion in 2022
content: Ukraine’s recently dismissed former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for a wartime presidential election in the most direct political challenge to Volodymyr Zelenskyy since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The politician, whose abrupt sacking last month triggered a wave of protests, said that Ukraine had to “restore a full democratic process even amid a prolonged war” in a video address released online late on Tuesday evening. “Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state,” Fedorov said in his nine-minute speech. Though he did not mention Zelenskyy by name, Fedorov implied the current president presided over a poorly functioning state that was struggling to tackle corruption despite the national emergency. “People cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made. Why some reforms move forward while others are blocked,” Fedorov said, arguing that Ukraine could fight a war and hold a national poll. “It is particularly dangerous when society develops the feeling that the main criterion for an appointment is not professionalism, results or the ability to transform the country, but personal loyalty to the system,” he said. Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there has been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while war continues. The US president, Donald Trump, has previously demanded that Ukraine hold an election, though his once-fraught relationship with Zelenskyy has gradually improved over the past year as Kyiv has shown it can hold its own on the battlefield. Fedorov, 35, was Ukraine’s digital minister from 2019 until January, fronting the country’s wartime adoption of drones, before briefly serving in what was considered to be a successful stint as defence minister until July. But he was suddenly dropped by Zelenskyy in a government reshuffle after a falling out with military commander Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi. Street protests followed, leading to the sacking of Syrskyi, but there was no sign Fedorov would be reinstated. On Tuesday Zelenskyy formally nominated Yevhen Khmara, the acting defence minister, to take the post permanently. Khmara’s nomination has to be confirmed by Ukraine’s parliament, and a vote is expected to take place on Wednesday. Artem Bronzhukov, a Ukrainian political analyst, questioned whether it would be practical to hold elections given that Russian bombing was continuing. “Today there is no clear understanding of how to ensure people’s safety in the context of a full-scale war,” he said. There was, he added, “a fairly deep-rooted view within Ukrainian society” that elections are necessary but only after the hot phase of the war ends – and that the country remained “a warring democracy – confirmed precisely by the protests taking place after Fedorov’s resignation from the government”. Protests had been taking place nightly in a square below the presidential office in the heart of Kyiv, but the numbers attending had been dwindling. However, the campaign was relaunched in a special rally on Sunday night that attracted about 2,000 people with regular chants of “Fedorov, Fedorov, Fedorov …” Polling conducted at the turn of the month reported the ex-minister would come third in the first round of a presidential election with 13.1%, behind Zelenskyy on 22.3% and the former head of the armed forces, who is now Ukraine’s ambassador to the UK, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, on 21.4%. The same polling, conducted by the Socis Centre for Social Research, also concluded that Zelenskyy would then be defeated in the run-off election by both Fedorov and Zaluzhnyi. Ukraine uses a two-stage voting system. If Ukraine were to hold an election, it would have to contend with the fact that millions have been exiled and displaced since the start of the war, and that more than 1 million are serving in the armed forces, many on the frontline. About a fifth of the country’s territory is also under Russian occupation.
chineseTitle: 乌克兰被解职的国防部长呼吁进行战时总统选举
chineseSummary: 米哈伊洛·费多罗夫的上诉是自 2022 年俄罗斯入侵以来对弗拉基米尔·泽伦斯基最直接的挑战
chineseContent: 乌克兰最近被解职的前国防部长米哈伊洛·费多罗夫呼吁举行战时总统选举，这是自俄罗斯于 2022 年开始全面入侵以来对弗拉基米尔·泽伦斯基最直接的政治挑战。这位政治家上个月突然被解职，引发了一波抗议活动，他在周二晚间发布的视频讲话中表示，乌克兰必须“在旷日持久的战争中恢复全面的民主进程”。 “民主不能被俄罗斯劫持。我们之所以战斗，正是因为我们想保持一个自由的欧洲国家，”费多罗夫在九分钟的演讲中说道。尽管费多罗夫没有提到泽连斯基的名字，但他暗示，现任总统领导的国家运转不善，尽管国家处于紧急状态，但仍在努力解决腐败问题。费多罗夫说：“人们不能无休止地生活在一种不理解为什么要做出某些决定的状态。为什么有些改革会取得进展，而另一些改革则会受到阻碍。”他认为乌克兰可以发动战争并举行全国大选。他说：“当社会认为任命的主要标准不是专业精神、成果或改造国家的能力，而是个人对制度的忠诚度时，这就特别危险了。”自俄罗斯全面入侵开始实施戒严以来，乌克兰的选举一直暂停。泽伦斯基的五年任期于 2024 年 5 月结束，但乌克兰几乎没有意愿在战争仍在继续的情况下举行竞选。美国总统唐纳德·特朗普此前曾要求乌克兰举行选举，尽管他与泽连斯基一度紧张的关系在过去一年中逐渐改善，因为基辅已经表明自己可以在战场上坚守自己的立场。费多罗夫，35 岁，乌克兰总统
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
